title: Shakalya's head falls off (3.9)
hook: the debate's last challenger keeps pushing, and the warning that stopped Gargi comes true for him
tomorrow: Janaka and Yajnavalkya: what is the light of man?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shakalya's countdown: 3,306 gods, then 33, then 6, 3, 2, one and a half, and one. Your line was one. Truth is one; the wise speak of it in many ways. Day three hundred eighty-one.

The title of today's chapter sounds like a horror film, and the text tells it in a single plain sentence. But first, the build-up. After the countdown, Shakalya doesn't sit down. He keeps firing questions: the gods of each direction, what the heart rests on, what the self is founded on. Yajnavalkya answers each one. And somewhere in the middle he stops and asks Shakalya something. Shakalya, have these scholars made you their coal-tongs? Their tool for pulling hot coals out of the fire, so they don't burn their own hands?
screen: `HE DOESN'T SIT DOWN.` → `QUESTION AFTER QUESTION.` → `HAVE THEY MADE YOU THEIR COAL-TONGS?`

segments.voice: That line tells you what's going on. Shakalya isn't Gargi, chasing a question to its edge. The others have sent him in to do the burning work for them. And he keeps going. So at last Yajnavalkya turns the debate around. Now I ask you, he says, about the person taught in the Upanishads, the one who leads all these out, brings them back, and goes beyond them. If you can't tell me who he is, your head will fall off. Shakalya didn't know. And his head fell off. The text adds one more grim line: thieves carried off his bones, thinking they were something else. Then nothing more is said of him. How to hear this? The text doesn't explain. Some readers take it literally, as the real stake of these Vedic debates. Others hear it as an image: his whole argument came apart; he lost face, the way we'd say it now. Either way, set it beside Gargi, a few days back. She got the very same warning, stopped, and came back later with better questions. Shakalya never stopped, and he was pushing as someone else's tool. Then the third book ends with a riddle. Yajnavalkya asks the room: a person is like a tree, hair for leaves, skin for bark. Cut a tree down, and it grows again from the root. From what root does a person grow, cut down by death? Nobody dares answer. The text answers instead: Brahman, which is knowing, which is joy.
screen: `SENT IN AS SOMEONE ELSE'S TOOL.` · `WHO IS THE PERSON OF THE UPANISHADS?` · `HE DIDN'T KNOW, AND HIS HEAD FELL.` · `FROM WHAT ROOT DOES A PERSON GROW?` · then, large: `DON'T ASK PAST THE LIMIT.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with the root. Sit, and breathe. Imagine yourself as a tree: hair like leaves, skin like bark, bones like the hard wood inside. Feel the weight of the body settle down into the seat, like roots into soil. Then ask the old riddle, without answering it: from what root do I grow? Let the question sit in the body, not the head. Breathe down into it. The bell holds the time.
Murdha, the head. The stake these debates put at risk, and for Shakalya the warning came true.
Your line: don't ask past the limit. Today, if you catch yourself asking a question to win rather than to know, stop, and ask a different one. Day three hundred eighty-one.

howItsDone: The Vedic brahmodya, a formal contest of questions about Brahman, is the setting of this chapter; teachers of the Upanishads read Shakalya's end alongside Gargi's warning, and the closing tree verses end the third book with a riddle.

fork.setup: you're Shakalya. Yajnavalkya has answered every question, and now he asks you about the person of the Upanishads, with your head as the stake. what happens?
options: Shakalya answers, and wins the cows.
Shakalya doesn't know, and his head falls off.
fork.reveal: he didn't know, and his head fell off. then Yajnavalkya asks the whole room the tree riddle, and nobody dares answer.

original.note: Sanskrit mūrdhan (nominative mūrdhā): the head, the top. the stake in the Brihadaranyaka's debates.

trapdoor: what you thought: a gruesome punishment for asking questions.
what it means: Shakalya pressed on as the others' tool, and couldn't answer the one question that mattered.
what a scholar hears: scholars link the head warning to the Vedic brahmodya contest; 3.9.26 asks about the aupaniṣada puruṣa, and 3.9.28's tree verses close the book.
